title: Anthropic IPO pitch highlights Dario Amodei's compute dilemma
excerpt: Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei details AI compute costs, IPO plans, and its cash buffer strategy with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon.
content_html:
CEO Dario Amodei says compute is the 'deepest business dilemma' facing Anthropic before its IPO

By Stephen Council

You're currently following this author! Click to unsubscribe from email alerts.

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei said a "huge uncertainty" around computing power is his company's "deepest business dilemma."

Amodei spoke in a Friday livestream with JPMorgan CEO Jamie Dimon ahead of Anthropic's coming initial public offering. The AI company is targeting a $1.4 trillion valuation and plans to start trading on Thursday.

Amodei pointed to his company's rapid growth and the quandary it poses: Anthropic has to predict how much computing power to buy for the years ahead, without under- or overspending. In an unproven industry, that's tricky.

"Because this field is growing so fast from a technological perspective, and we don't know how that is going to transfer to the creation of economic value on the business side, we have this huge uncertainty," Amodei said.

He added that the task gets trickier over time because the costs grow larger each year. Anthropic, in its IPO prospectus, disclosed that it has committed around $900 billion in infrastructure investments, with around half due by 2030.

If Anthropic buys more compute than it needs, its costs could race dangerously far ahead of its revenues. And if it underspends, Amodei said, the company could find itself unable to deliver to customers all the AI they're demanding, or to conduct research and development to create the next AI model.

"It's a very difficult problem," Amodei told Dimon.

Anthropic has two forms of 'buffer'

Anthropic will try to make accurate demand forecasts based on the momentum it sees for new products and hits like Claude Code.

Amodei also outlined the two ways his company is facing down the inherent uncertainty around compute.

One of them is the company's gross margins. Amodei praised the amount of money his company has been able to wring from each unit of compute. Analysts see this metric as one of the most important to watch for understanding Anthropic's strength.

The other, Amodei said, is Anthropic's cash. The IPO prospectus said that as of September 30, the company had more than $95 billion in cash and cash equivalents, plus another $36 billion in short-term investments. The IPO will funnel billions more dollars into the company's coffers.

He said that Anthropic's strategy is to buy "relatively little" compute in advance, setting the company up well if demand lags. If demand runs higher, he said, the company has the cash to buy compute on the spot market — a short-term, immediate option.

Amodei said that he's confident that "for periods of time where things don't go as well, we're well covered, and we're well insulated."

Anthropic plans to set its price on Wednesday and then begin trading on Thursday of next week.
